perhaps in Latin

perhaps

fortasse

Ancient LatinQuotationsComposed phrasesDraft
  • fortasse — maybe, perhaps classical (Cic. Div. Caec. 40: fortasse dīcēs)1 The everyday word of Cicero’s prose, with the indicative.
  • forsitan — perhaps classical also used (Cic. Rosc. Am. 5: forsitan quaerātis) From fors sit an; in Cicero always with the subjunctive.
  • forsan — perhaps (vōx plērumque poētica: Verg., Hor.; also post-Augustan prose) classical also used (Verg. A. 1.203)
  • fortassis — perhaps; the same word as fortasse, rarer classical also used (Plaut.; Cic.; Hor.)
  • forsan et haec ōlim meminisse juvābit — perhaps one day even this will be a pleasure to remember (Verg. A. 1.203)
  • Fortasse. — Maybe (as an answer). composed
  • Fortasse pluet; paenulam indue. — Maybe it’ll rain; put your coat on. composed
  • Veniētne avia? — Fortasse. — Is Grandma coming? — Maybe. composed
  1. Why fortasse, not fortassē: Lewis & Short prints a long final e but gives no evidence. De Vaan (2008: 236, s.v. fors) speaks of the word’s “short final vowel”, and verse proves it. In Catullus 85.1, Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam fortasse requīris, the fifth foot -tasse re- must be a dactyl, so the e is short; Horace scans it the same way (S. 1.3.20, 1.6.98). Ruling: fortasse with a short final e
